summary: Describes the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP), which connects multiple IPv4 PIM Sparse-Mode domains. Each domain keeps its own Rendezvous Point and need not depend on those of other domains. The RFC is experimental and documents what existing MSDP implementations already do.

eli5.summary: Imagine several towns that each run their own radio station. This lets the stations tell each other who is broadcasting, so listeners in any town can tune into shows from another town.

questions: how do pim sm domains share multicast sources
subtitle: How rendezvous points in separate multicast domains tell each other which sources are active.

tldr.problem: Each PIM Sparse-Mode domain has its own Rendezvous Point (RP), but receivers in one domain cannot join a source that registered at an RP in another domain unless the RPs share what they know.
tldr.mechanism: RPs form MSDP peerings over TCP and flood Source-Active (SA) messages that announce active (source, group) pairs. Peers forward each SA by a peer-RPF check, and an interested RP then joins the source tree toward the source.
tldr.outcome: Each domain can keep its own independent RP without relying on third-party RPs. The RFC is Experimental and documents what existing MSDP implementations already did.

today: RFC 3618 is an Experimental RFC from October 2003 that documents existing MSDP implementations, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It says MSDP is used primarily between PIM domains and between Anycast-RPs (RFC 3446) within a domain.

sections.title: Connecting PIM-SM Domains
sections.content:
The Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) connects multiple IPv4 PIM Sparse-Mode (PIM-SM) domains. Each domain uses its own independent RP and does not depend on RPs in other domains. The RFC lists two advantages: no third-party resource dependencies on a domain's RP, and receiver-only domains that get data without globally advertising group membership.

MSDP-speaking routers in a domain peer with MSDP peers in other domains. Each peering is a TCP connection carrying control information, and together the peerings form a virtual topology whose purpose is to let domains discover sources elsewhere. If a source is of interest, normal PIM-SM source-tree building delivers the data over an inter-domain tree. MSDP may be used with protocols other than PIM-SM, but that is not specified here.
sections.eli5: Each town keeps its own station manager. The managers phone each other so every town knows which shows are on air.

sections.title: Flood-and-Join Procedure
sections.content:
When an RP first learns of a new sender, for example through PIM register messages, it builds a Source-Active (SA) message carrying the source address, the group address and its own RP address, and sends it to its MSDP peers. Only RPs may originate SAs, and an RP originates one only for a source that would register to it. Intermediate MSDP speakers MAY forward SAs from other domains but do not originate them for sources elsewhere.

A receiving RP checks for a (*,G) entry with a non-empty outgoing interface list. If it finds one, it triggers an (S,G) join toward the source, building a branch of the source tree to its domain; data then arrives at the RP and flows down the domain's shared tree. If an RP later receives a PIM Join for a new group G, it SHOULD trigger an (S,G) join for each active (S,G) of that group in its SA cache. The RFC calls this flood-and-join: an RP not interested in a group simply ignores the SA.

An MSDP speaker MUST cache SA messages. Caching paces messages, reduces join latency for new receivers, helps debugging, and limits SA storms by not forwarding SAs that are not new or already cached. An RP MAY also encapsulate the first multicast data in an SA so that bursts are not lost while the tree is built; implementations MUST bound how long they encapsulate.
sections.eli5: When a new show starts, the local station manager shouts about it to the other managers. A manager whose town wants it tunes in; the others ignore the news.

sections.title: Peer-RPF Forwarding and Mesh Groups
sections.content:
SAs are forwarded using a peer-RPF check, which compares the RP address in the SA with the peer the message came from, using the Multicast RPF Routing Information Base (MRIB). An SA from R received by X from N is accepted only if N is X's peer-RPF neighbor for R; otherwise it is dropped. An accepted SA is forwarded to all other MSDP peers.

The neighbor is chosen by the first matching rule: N is R itself; N is the eBGP next hop of the route to R; N advertised the route to R (iBGP advertiser, or IGP next hop for link-state routing); N is in the closest AS on the best path to R, with the highest IP address winning ties; or N is configured as the static RPF peer. Peers not in ESTABLISHED state are not eligible.

A mesh group reduces flooding, typically inside a domain, when some MSDP speakers form a full mesh. A member that receives an SA from another member accepts it but MUST NOT forward it to other members of the group, since the originator already sent it to all of them. Filtering policy should generally be expressed with MBGP, and transit domains should not filter SAs, or sources may not be known everywhere. An SA for (S,G) MUST NOT be sent to peers across an administrative scope boundary for G.
sections.eli5: To avoid the same news going round in circles, each manager only believes news that arrives from the direction of the manager who first announced it. Managers in a tight group tell each other directly and do not repeat it.

sections.title: Connections, Timers and the State Machine
sections.content:
MSDP runs over TCP on well-known port 639. In each peering the peer with the higher IP address listens and the other connects actively, which avoids call collision. The cost is that startup depends entirely on the active side and its connect retry timer. A peer starts in DISABLED and moves through INACTIVE, LISTEN or CONNECTING to ESTABLISHED.

  • SA-Advertisement-Period MUST be 60 seconds; an RP spreads its periodic SAs over that interval and MUST NOT send more than one periodic SA per (S,G) in it.
  • HoldTime-Period MUST be at least three seconds; 75 seconds is recommended.
  • KeepAlive-Period MUST be less than the hold time and at least one second; 60 seconds is recommended.
  • ConnectRetry-Period SHOULD be 30 seconds.

Each SA cache entry has an SA-State timer, and the state period MUST NOT be less than the SA-Advertisement-Period plus the SA-Hold-Down-Period. A TLV format error SHOULD reset the session; other errors such as an unrecognized type code SHOULD cause the message to be silently discarded without a reset.
sections.eli5: Two managers set up a phone line; the one with the bigger number waits for the call. They send quick hello signals so each knows the other is still on the line.

sections.title: TLV Format and Source-Active Messages
sections.content:
All MSDP messages are TLVs: an 8-bit Type, a 16-bit Length covering type, length and value, and a variable Value. The maximum TLV length is 9192. Defined types are 1 IPv4 Source-Active, 2 Source-Active Request, 3 Source-Active Response, 4 KeepAlive and 5 reserved (previously Notification); 6 and 7 are MSDP traceroute types assigned but not described.

An IPv4 Source-Active TLV holds an Entry Count, the RP Address, and for each entry a reserved field, a Sprefix Len that MUST be sent as 32, a Group Address and a Source Address. Several (S,G) pairs from one RP can be batched at the expense of latency. The length can also cover an encapsulated IPv4 packet, in which case only the last entry may carry data. A KeepAlive TLV is just type 4 with length 3 and is sent only if nothing else was sent to the peer within the KeepAlive period.

The IANA now manages an MSDP TLV Values namespace: values 8 to 200 need IESG Approval or Standards Action, and 201 to 255 are for experimental use.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a tag saying what kind it is and how long it is. The main one is a list saying who is broadcasting what, and where.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An MSDP implementation MUST implement Keyed MD5 (RFC 2385) to secure control messages and MUST be able to interoperate with peers that do not support it. If only one side is configured with Keyed MD5, the connection SHOULD NOT be established.

To limit state explosion during denial of service and other attacks, SA filters and limits SHOULD be used, such as access lists of sources or groups, a cap on SA-state entries, or a rate limit on creating new SA state. The RFC adds that if follow-on work is done, a more robust integrity mechanism such as HMAC-SHA1 ought to be employed.
sections.eli5: The managers check a secret code on each phone call, and they limit how much news they will accept so nobody can flood them.

fields.name: Length (x + y)
fields.desc: Control information length x plus encapsulated packet length y.

fields.name: Entry Count
fields.desc: Number of (S,G) entries that follow the RP address.

fields.name: RP Address
fields.desc: Address of the RP in the domain where the source became active.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Sent as zeros and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Sprefix Len
fields.desc: Route prefix length for the source address.

fields.name: Group Address
fields.desc: Group the active source sent data to.

fields.name: Source Address
fields.desc: IP address of the active source.
